steps.message:
The weather and air stations of a regional network upload their logger dumps to /app/data. Write a Python script at /app/bin/hourly.py that turns the dumps into the hourly station product by the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md) and writes the hourly file described in /app/docs/output.md. It is run as `python3 /app/bin/hourly.py INPUT_DIR OUTPUT_FILE`. Run it on /app/data and save the result as /app/out/hourly.json.

From /app, `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .` runs the script on a few small inputs, and `python tools/check_hourly.py` compares /app/out/hourly.json with the approved hourly values for the current dumps. The script will also be run on dumps from other stations and other periods, so it must follow the documented rules rather than what the current files happen to contain. Use only the Python standard library. Do not change anything under /app/data, /app/docs, /app/tests or /app/tools.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

<path>docs/overview.md</path>
<content>
1 	# Hourly station product: overview
2 	
3 	The weather and air stations of the network sample their sensors every few
4 	seconds or minutes and keep the readings in a logger. When a logger gets a
5 	connection it uploads what it holds as a text file, a logger dump. The hourly
6 	product turns all dumps of all stations into one value per station, hour and
7 	quantity, which the forecasting and air quality teams load as it is.
8 	
9 	This note says what goes in, what comes out and in which order the work is
10	done. The rules for each step live in their own notes:
11	
12	| Note | Covers |
13	|---|---|
14	| `files.md` | logger dumps: lines, directives, data rows, missing values |
15	| `clock.md` | logger time zones, clock drift and sync lines, repeated rows |
16	| `quantities.md` | the quantities, their units and conversions, valid ranges |
17	| `aggregation.md` | hours, coverage, means, wind direction, rain |
18	| `output.md` | the hourly file |
19	| `changelog.md` | what changed between versions of these rules |
20	
21	Where this note and a numbered rule in another note seem to disagree, the
22	numbered rule wins. The rules apply to every station and every period the
23	same way: nothing in them depends on a particular station, logger, file or
24	date.
25	
26	## 1. Inputs
27	
28	1.1 An input directory holds logger dumps: every regular file in it whose
29	name ends in `.log`. Other files are not dumps and are ignored. The directory
30	has no subdirectories that matter.
31	
32	1.2 A station uploads many dumps. Dumps overlap in time, and a logger can
33	upload a period again later with some values changed (a reissue). The file
34	name says nothing reliable about the station, the period or the order of the
35	uploads; the directives inside the file do (`files.md` 3).
36	
37	## 2. Steps
38	
39	1. Read every dump (`files.md`), converting each value to its canonical unit
40	   (`quantities.md` 2) and dropping values that are missing or out of range
41	   (`files.md` 6, `quantities.md` 3).
42	2. Put the logger time of every row on UTC (`clock.md` 1).
43	3. Keep one row per station and logger instant (`clock.md` 3).
44	4. Correct every row for clock drift (`clock.md` 2).
45	5. Assign each row to its hour (`aggregation.md` 1) and compute the hourly
46	   values (`aggregation.md` 2 to 5).
47	
48	Then write every hour of every station to one file (`output.md`).
49	
50	## 3. Terms
51	
52	- A **logger time** is a date and time as the logger's clock showed it, in
53	  the logger's own time zone (`clock.md` 1).
54	- The **logger UTC instant** of a row is its logger time moved to UTC with the
55	  `tz` of its file. It still carries the logger's clock error.
56	- The **corrected time** of a row is its logger UTC instant plus the clock
57	  offset at that instant (`clock.md` 2). It is the best estimate of when the
58	  reading was taken.
59	- A **reading** of a quantity is one value in one data row that is not
60	  missing and is inside the valid range of the quantity.
61	- The **interval** of a station is the time between two readings of its
62	  logger, in seconds.
63	
64	## 4. Running the program
65	
66	4.1 The program reads one input directory and writes one hourly file:
67	
68	    python3 /app/bin/hourly.py INPUT_DIR OUTPUT_FILE
69	
70	It uses only the Python standard library, reads nothing outside `INPUT_DIR`
71	and writes nothing but `OUTPUT_FILE`. The same input gives the same output
72	wherever the input directory is.
73	
74	4.2 The dumps are well formed: every data row has one field per column of
75	its `columns` line, every directive the rules require is present, and every
76	time is a real date and time. A program does not have to check this.
</content>

<path>docs/clock.md</path>
<content>
1 	# Logger clocks
2 	
3 	## 1. Logger time zones
4 	
5 	1.1 A logger clock runs on a fixed offset from UTC, with no daylight saving
6 	time. The `tz` directive of a file gives it: `Z` for UTC, or a sign, hours
7 	and minutes, `+HH:MM` or `-HH:MM`. Offsets need not be whole hours
8 	(`+05:30`, `-03:30`).
9 	
10	1.2 The logger UTC instant of a logger time is the logger time minus the
11	offset: 10:00:00 at `+02:00` is 08:00:00 UTC, 10:00:00 at `-03:30` is
12	13:30:00 UTC.
13	
14	1.3 Every row and every sync line uses the `tz` of its own file. A logger can
15	be set to another time zone between two uploads, so two files of one station
16	can state different `tz` values, and the same reading can appear in both
17	with different logger times.
18	
19	## 2. Clock drift
20	
21	2.1 Logger clocks gain or lose a few seconds a day. When a logger reaches the
22	network time service it writes a sync line (`files.md` 7): `logger=` is what
23	its clock showed at that moment, and `ref=` is the true UTC time at the same
24	moment. The logger does not set its clock from it; a sync line is a
25	comparison only.
26	
27	2.2 The offset at a sync point is `ref` minus the logger UTC instant of
28	`logger=`, in whole seconds. It can be negative. In the example of `files.md`
29	the logger time 09:12:41 at `+01:00` is 08:12:41 UTC and `ref` is 08:12:03,
30	so the offset is -38 seconds.
31	
32	2.3 The sync points of a station are collected from all of its files. A sync
33	point that appears in several files (overlapping or reissued uploads) counts
34	once; it is identified by its logger UTC instant, and if two files disagree
35	on its `ref`, the file with the larger upload number is right.
36	
37	2.4 The clock offset at a logger UTC instant `t`:
38	
39	- At a sync point, the offset of that sync point.
40	- Between two consecutive sync points `(t1, o1)` and `(t2, o2)`, with
41	  `t1 < t < t2`: `o1 + (o2 - o1) * (t - t1) / (t2 - t1)`, rounded down to a
42	  whole second. Rounded down means toward negative infinity, also when the
43	  result is negative: -12.4 becomes -13.
44	- Before the first sync point of the station, the offset of the first sync
45	  point; after the last, the offset of the last. Offsets are never
46	  extrapolated.
47	- A station without any sync point has offset 0 everywhere.
48	
49	2.5 The corrected time of a row is its logger UTC instant plus the clock
50	offset at that instant. Hours (`aggregation.md` 1), the order of rain
51	readings (`aggregation.md` 5) and the range of hours of a station
52	(`output.md` 2.2) all use corrected times.
53	
54	## 3. Repeated rows
55	
56	3.1 Dumps overlap, because a logger sends again what it is not sure was
57	received, and a logger can reissue a period with corrected values. Two rows of
58	one station with the same logger UTC instant are the same sample.
59	
60	3.2 Of the rows of one sample, only the row from the file with the largest
61	upload number is kept. It is kept as a whole: its missing values stay
62	missing, even where an older file had a value. The other rows of the sample
63	are dropped.
64	
65	3.3 Repeated rows are found by logger UTC instant, not by the logger time as
66	written, since files of one station can use different `tz` values (rule 1.3).
</content>

1 	# Changelog of the hourly rules
2 	
3 	## 4.0 (2027-03)
4 	
5 	- Coverage is enough at 75 percent of the expected count (`aggregation.md`
6 	  2.2). Up to 3.x the threshold was 60 percent, and the air quality team
7 	  found hourly means built from a little more than half an hour of samples
8 	  that did not match the station's own displays.
9 	- Repeated rows are found by logger UTC instant (`clock.md` 3.3). Up to 3.x
10	  they were found by the logger time as written, which kept both copies of
11	  every sample uploaded before and after a logger changed its time zone.
12	
13	## 3.2 (2026-11)
14	
15	- Clock offsets between sync points are rounded down (`clock.md` 2.4). 3.1
16	  rounded them to the nearest second; 3.0 cut off the decimals, which rounds
17	  negative offsets up.
18	- Offsets are held at the first and last sync point (`clock.md` 2.4). 3.1
19	  extrapolated the line through the two nearest sync points, which moved the
20	  first and last hours of a station by minutes when its logger was slow to
21	  reach the time service.
22	
23	## 3.1 (2026-07)
24	
25	- A reissued row replaces the older row as a whole (`clock.md` 3.2). 3.0
26	  took each field from the newest file that had a value for it, which brought
27	  back values the station operator had withdrawn.
28	- Wind direction is a vector mean of unit vectors, calm samples left out
29	  (`aggregation.md` 4). Up to 3.0 it was the arithmetic mean of the angles,
30	  which gave 180 for winds between 350 and 10 degrees.
31	
32	## 3.0 (2026-03)
33	
34	- Hours are named by their end (`aggregation.md` 1.1), as the forecasting
35	  system names them. Up to 2.x an hour was named by its start.
36	- Rain is worked out from counter increments, with restarts and gaps
37	  (`aggregation.md` 5). Up to 2.x the gauges reported a total per sample.
38	
39	## 2.0 (2025-10)
40	
41	- `units` lines can appear inside a file and set only the quantities they
42	  name (`files.md` 4.2). Sensors are swapped in the field without a new
43	  upload.
</content>

1 	# Hourly values
2 	
3 	## 1. Hours
4 	
5 	1.1 An hour is named by the UTC time at which it ends. Hour `H` holds the
6 	corrected times after `H` minus one hour, up to and including `H`. A reading
7 	with corrected time 10:00:00 belongs to hour 10:00; one at 10:00:01 belongs
8 	to hour 11:00; one at 09:00:00 belongs to hour 09:00.
9 	
10	1.2 Hours are always on UTC, whatever the `tz` of the files.
11	
12	## 2. Coverage
13	
14	2.1 For each station, hour and quantity, `n` is the number of readings of
15	the quantity in the hour (rows kept after `clock.md` 3, values not missing,
16	inside the valid range). The expected count of an hour is 3600 divided by
17	the interval of the station.
18	
19	2.2 The hourly value of a quantity is reported only when coverage is enough:
20	`n` must be at least 75 percent of the expected count, that is `n * 4 >= expected * 3`; otherwise the value is null and `n` is still reported.
21	
22	2.3 Drift correction can move a sample into the next or previous hour, so an
23	hour can hold one reading more or less than the expected count. That changes
24	nothing in rule 2.2.
25	
26	## 3. Means
27	
28	3.1 The hourly value of `temp`, `rh`, `pres` and `wspd` is the arithmetic
29	mean of the readings of the hour, in the canonical unit.
30	
31	## 4. Wind direction
32	
33	4.1 The hourly value of `wdir` is a vector mean, never an arithmetic mean of
34	the angles: each reading of `wdir` whose row also has a reading of `wspd`
35	greater than 0 gives a unit vector pointing to its direction. The hourly
36	direction is the direction of the sum of these vectors, in degrees clockwise
37	from north, from 0 up to but not including 360. Wind speeds do not weight the
38	vectors.
39	
40	4.2 `n` of `wdir` counts every reading of `wdir` of the hour, calm samples
41	and samples without a `wspd` reading included. Coverage (rule 2.2) is
42	checked on that `n`.
43	
44	4.3 When coverage is enough but no reading of the hour gives a vector (every
45	sample calm or without a `wspd` reading), the value is null.
46	
47	## 5. Rain
48	
49	5.1 A rain gauge reports a counter that grows with each tip of its bucket and
50	goes back to 0 when the logger restarts. The hourly value of `rain` is the
51	precipitation of the hour in millimetres, worked out from the increments of
52	the counter.
53	
54	5.2 The readings of `rain` of a station are taken in corrected time order.
55	For each reading `r` with a previous reading `p`, if the corrected times of
56	`p` and `r` are at most 2.5 intervals apart, `r` has an increment:
57	`r - p` when `r >= p`, and `r` itself when `r < p` (the counter restarted at 0
58	since `p`). A reading without a previous reading, or with one that is more
59	than 2.5 intervals before it, has no increment: what fell during the gap is
60	not known.
61	
62	5.3 Missing and out of range values are not readings, so `p` is the last
63	reading before `r`, however many rows without a rain reading lie between.
64	
65	5.4 The hourly value is the sum of the increments of the readings in the
66	hour. `n` counts the readings of the hour, with or without an increment, and
67	coverage is rule 2.2. An hour with enough coverage and no rain has the value
68	0.
